In 1900, Max Planck was trying to solve a stubborn problem: the spectrum of radiation emitted by a hot body.

The mathematics led him somewhere unexpected.

He found that the observed spectrum could be explained if energy were exchanged not continuously, but in discrete packets:

E = hν

Here, ν is frequency and h is the constant now bearing his name.

Planck initially treated quantization as a mathematical necessity rather than a complete new picture of nature. But the small constant h became one of the defining constants of modern physics.

Einstein soon pushed the idea further by treating light itself as quantized.

A problem about thermal radiation had opened the door to quantum theory.

Source: Nobel Prize, historical account of the development of quantum theory and Planck’s 1900 work.

The strange thing about the zeta function is that Euler found its connection to primes long before anyone knew how deep it went.

In 1737, Euler showed that

ζ(s) = ∏p 1/(1 − p⁻ˢ)

linking an infinite sum over all integers directly to the prime numbers. More than a century later, Riemann extended the function into the complex plane in 1859 and asked where its nontrivial zeros lie.

That question became the Riemann Hypothesis, still one of mathematics’ great unsolved problems.

I understood the Hessian much better when I stopped thinking of it as a matrix of second derivatives.

Think about a loss surface near some point in parameter space.

Pick a unit direction u and move along it. At that point, the second directional derivative of the loss is

u^T H u

where H is the Hessian.

Now the eigenvectors of H become interesting.

If vᵢ is a unit eigenvector, then

vᵢ^T H vᵢ = λᵢ

So the corresponding eigenvalue gives the local curvature along that eigenvector direction.

A positive eigenvalue close to zero means relatively weak curvature. A larger positive eigenvalue means the surface bends much more sharply in that direction.

This also helps explain why optimization can become difficult when curvature varies greatly across directions. Locally, a learning rate that behaves well along a flatter direction can be too aggressive along a sharply curved one.

The Hessian is not just a table of second derivatives.

It describes the local second-order geometry of the loss surface.

WHAT IF SOMEWHERE IN THE UNIVERSE, ANOTHER VERSION OF YOU IS LIVING A DIFFERENT LIFE?

It sounds like something from a science-fiction movie. But a real idea in quantum physics leaves open a possibility that is even stranger.

In 1957, physicist Hugh Everett proposed what became known as the Many-Worlds Interpretation of quantum mechanics. Instead of saying that a quantum system picks one outcome when it is measured, the idea says that all possible outcomes can continue to exist in separate branches of reality.

And if that sounds difficult to imagine, take it one step further.

Suppose a quantum event could unfold in two different ways. In the Many-Worlds picture, reality does not necessarily choose just one and erase the other. The different outcomes become separated into different branches through a process called quantum decoherence.

As those branches continue to develop, their histories can become completely different.

One branch could contain a version of events where something happened one way. Another could contain a different outcome. And, in principle, those different histories could include different versions of the people living through them.

So there could be a version of you whose life took a different path.

But there is no way to meet that person or send them a message. The branches are expected to become effectively separate and unable to interact with each other.

And this is where the story needs a reality check.

Scientists have not found another universe containing another Earth or another version of you. Many-Worlds is an interpretation of quantum mechanics, not experimental proof that parallel worlds exist.

Other interpretations explain the same quantum experiments without requiring an ever-branching reality.

Still, the idea raises a question that is hard to shake.

What if reality is far bigger than the single version of it we can experience?

What if every moment where several outcomes were possible did not simply end with one choice?

What if, somewhere beyond our ability to observe, the other possibilities continued too?

We don’t know.

And perhaps that is the strangest part of all.

Source: Hugh Everett, Relative State Formulation of Quantum Mechanics (1957); research on quantum decoherence and interpretations of quantum mechanics.

2 · 7! = 10080, the exact number of minutes in a week.

Regroup the factors and the calendar appears: 2 · 7! = 7 × (4 · 3 · 2) × (6 · 5 · 2) = 7 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes.

It works because 24 and 60 were chosen to be highly divisible, so they split neatly into small factors. That is the same reason clocks, angles and Babylonian astronomy use 60.

The trick repeats: 6! hours = 30 days, and 10! seconds = 6 weeks exactly.

Which other unit hides a factorial?

Great paper from ByteDance Seed on Block-Sparse Attention.

So many papers wave their hands and claim sparse attention scales linearly, but if you look under the hood, the block selection step almost always quietly ruins the party. 

Sure, once you identify the top-K blocks, the attention computation itself is cheap. 

But deciding which blocks deserve that attention usually means scoring every query against every key block across the sequence. 

That leaves you stuck with an O(N^2) bottleneck anyway, which completely defeats the purpose once you push context lengths out to the extreme.

The authors tackle that search problem with a framework they call PISA. 

Instead of doing a brute force sweep over every block candidate, they set up a coarse to fine pyramid of keys. 

You do an initial, cheap check at the coarsest level using pooled keys, throw out the irrelevant chunks, and only drill down into finer granularities for the candidates that actually scored well. 

By bounding the candidate set at each stage across O(\log N) levels, they pull the entire selection and compute cost down to genuine O(N \log N) complexity.

They implemented custom Triton kernels for both training and inference that fuse the hierarchical routing with the LogSumExp scoring, avoiding materializing the big query-key intermediate matrices entirely. 

On standard benchmarks it holds parity with dense models, but where it actually shines is retrieval, which makes total sense given the hierarchical search setup.

It feels obvious in hindsight, hierarchical spatial search is an old concept in graphics and classical algorithms, but seeing it executed cleanly in modern attention kernels is really satisfying to read. 

Definitely worth a look if you care about efficient long context architectures: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.31093

In theoretical physics, particularly in general relativity, string theory, and condensed matter physics, transverse traceless (TT) gravitons and gapless modes are deeply interconnected concepts. They both describe excitations that can propagate over long distances without requiring a minimum threshold of energy.
Here is a breakdown of how these two concepts relate and what they mean.
------------------------------
## 1. Transverse Traceless (TT) Gravitons
In general relativity, when we look at weak gravitational fields rippling through spacetime (gravitational waves), we perturb the flat metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ by a small amount $h_{\mu\nu}$. Because general relativity has coordinate freedom (gauge symmetry), we can choose a specific gauge to simplify the mathematics.
This is the Transverse Traceless (TT) gauge, which isolates the physical, propagating degrees of freedom of the graviton. It satisfies two conditions:

* Transverse: $\partial^\mu h_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (The wave propagates perpendicular to its oscillations, like light).
* Traceless: $h^\mu_\mu = 0$ (The metric perturbation does not change the local volume).

## 2. What are Gapless Modes?
In quantum field theory and condensed matter physics, a gapless mode (or massless excitation) is a state where the energy (E) goes to zero as the momentum (p) goes to zero.

* Gapped mode: Requires a minimum energy injection (E = m c²) to excite the particle at rest (e.g., a massive Higgs boson).
* Gapless mode: Can be excited with infinitely small energy (e.g., a photon or a phonon).

## 3. The Connection: TT Gravitons as Gapless Modes
The transverse traceless graviton is the quintessential example of a tensor gapless mode.
## Goldstone's Theorem & Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
In many physical systems, gapless modes arise because a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken (becoming Nambu-Goldstone bosons).

* Photons are gapless modes protecting the U(1) gauge symmetry.
* Phonons (sound waves) are gapless modes arising from breaking translational symmetry in a crystal lattice.
* Gravitons can be viewed as the gapless Goldstone-like modes resulting from the spontaneous breaking of Lorentz/diffeomorphism invariance by the presence of a background spacetime metric.

## Dispersion Relation
Because the TT graviton is gapless, its dispersion relation is linear:
$$E = c\vert{}\vec{p}\vert{}$$ 
This implies that gravitons are massless and travel precisely at the speed of light (c). If the graviton had a "gap" (a mass), gravitational waves would travel slower than light, and gravity would have a finite range instead of an infinite one.

Security starts with the basics.

A secure system is rarely protected by one tool. It is protected by layers that verify users, control access, protect data, and reduce exposure.

Here are 11 system security concepts every engineer should understand:

1. Authentication → Verify who the user is before granting access.
2. Authorization → Check what the user is allowed to do.
3. OAuth 2.0 → Give apps limited access using scopes and tokens.
4. OpenID Connect → Add identity verification on top of OAuth.
5. JWT → Use signed tokens for stateless authentication.
6. Session Management → Keep user sessions secure across requests.
7. TLS Everywhere → Encrypt traffic to prevent interception and tampering.
8. Secrets Management → Store, rotate, and securely inject credentials.
9. Role-Based Access Control → Assign permissions based on roles and least privilege.
10. Network Isolation → Separate network layers to reduce exposure and lateral movement.
11. Zero Trust → Continuously verify identity, device, context, and access.

The value comes from how these concepts work together.

Authentication proves identity. Authorization decides permissions. TLS protects data in transit. Secrets management protects credentials. Network isolation limits exposure. Zero Trust keeps verification continuous.

Strong security is not one feature added at the end. It is a system where every request, token, permission, and connection is checked at the right layer.
